opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so it really starts before the weights are even public in a lot of cases. We work closely with model providers, so when a new model is coming, the first thing we do is understand the architecture: is it a dense model or a mixture of experts, what's the attention mechanism, how long is the context window, are there any new operators we haven't seen before? That tells us how much of our existing stack carries over and where we need to write new kernels or change how we shard the model across GPUs.

Then there's correctness, which people underestimate. Before we think about speed at all, we have to make sure our implementation matches the reference: same outputs, same quality on benchmarks, tokenizer and chat template handled exactly right. A lot of the "this model is worse than advertised" complaints you see online come from small serving bugs, like a wrong template or a numerical issue in a custom kernel. So we invest heavily in evals at that stage.

Once it's correct, we move to performance. That's where our optimization work comes in: picking the right parallelism strategy, quantization where it doesn't hurt quality, speculative decoding, caching, and tuning batching for different traffic shapes. And the important point is there's no single best configuration. A customer building a real-time voice agent cares about latency, someone running batch document processing cares about throughput and cost. So we profile across those tradeoffs and expose the right options.

Finally, there's the operational side: capacity planning, autoscaling, monitoring, making sure it holds up under real production load on day one, not just in a demo. Our goal is that when a model launches, developers can hit an API and get something fast, reliable, and faithful to the original model, and then customize or fine-tune on top of it. Day-zero launches get the headlines, but the real work is making it production-grade.

r001.rationale: It says the team examines each model’s architecture, then decides what existing stack applies and where to add kernels or change GPU sharding.

r002.rationale: It identifies a numerical issue in a custom kernel as a serving bug that can make a model seem worse than advertised.

r003.rationale: It describes checking implementation correctness for a new model, but does not state that capabilities layered on top of raw inference must each be validated for that model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, because it's actually a pretty intense process, and a lot of it happens before the model is even public. With the big open model releases, we usually get early access from the model developers, sometimes a few days, sometimes a few weeks ahead. So our first job is just getting the architecture to run at all. Every new generation brings something new: a different attention variant, mixture of experts with a different routing scheme, a new tokenizer, multimodal encoders bolted on. Our kernel team has to look at that and figure out what we already support out of the box and what needs new kernels or new fusion patterns.

Then there's correctness, which people underestimate. We're running a custom serving stack, so we have to verify that what we produce matches the reference implementation numerically, and then that it still matches once we turn on quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, all the optimizations that make it fast and cheap. We run eval suites, we diff outputs against the reference, and we're pretty paranoid about it, because a subtle bug in a kernel can look fine on a quick test and then degrade quality in a way customers only notice weeks later.

After that it's performance work. We profile on the actual hardware we'll serve on, we look at where the time goes for different traffic shapes, long context versus short, high batch versus latency sensitive, and we tune from there. And we think about the serving configuration too, how many GPUs per replica, what parallelism strategy, where the memory goes.

And then finally the boring but important part: the API, the function calling, structured outputs, making sure the chat template behaves, and scaling the capacity so that when it launches and everybody hits it at once, it holds up. Launch day traffic is always a spike, so we plan for that explicitly. Honestly, the goal is that on day one, a developer can just swap the model name and it works, and all that complexity is invisible to them.

r001.rationale: The response describes checking which serving components already support each model’s architecture and adding model-specific kernels or fusion patterns, along with tuning its serving configuration.

r002.rationale: It says numerical output must match the reference and warns that a subtle kernel bug can degrade model quality, identifying an inference-component correctness issue as a cause of degradation.

r003.rationale: For each new model, it validates numerical correctness against the reference after enabling quantization, speculative decoding, prefix caching, and other serving optimizations.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as two parts: getting the model running correctly, and getting it running well in production. First, we want to understand the model’s architecture, its dependencies, and the hardware it needs. We establish a baseline so that, as we optimize, we can check that we’re preserving the model’s behavior.

Then we look at performance under realistic workloads. What do the inputs look like? How much concurrency do we expect? What are the latency requirements? Those questions guide decisions around batching, memory management, and optimizations like quantization. You’re balancing latency, throughput, cost, and quality.

Before launch, we also need to understand how it behaves under load and when something fails. Can we scale it reliably? Can we observe what’s happening and roll back if necessary? Getting a model to produce an answer is the starting point. Getting it to serve users consistently is what makes it ready to launch.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding the model’s architecture, dependencies, and hardware, but does not describe assembling inference-engine building blocks selected for that model.

r002.rationale: It mentions preserving model behavior during optimization, but does not identify numerical errors from assembling inference-engine components as a potential cause of accuracy degradation.

r003.rationale: It recommends establishing a baseline to check behavior during optimization, but does not state that capabilities layered on raw inference need correctness validation for each model.

sol-6.1.text:
We start with the use case: what latency does the application need, what throughput do we need to support, and what does good model quality look like? Those requirements guide how we serve the model, because there isn’t one configuration that works best for every workload.

Then we profile it on the target hardware and test the serving configuration—things like batching, precision, and how the model is distributed across GPUs. The key is to measure those choices against realistic traffic. A configuration that looks great in a benchmark may behave very differently when requests have different input and output lengths.

Before launching, we want confidence in both performance and reliability. We load-test, check failure behavior, and roll out gradually with monitoring. Getting a model to run is the starting point; getting it to serve consistently at the right cost is what makes it ready for production.

r001.rationale: The response describes profiling and tuning serving settings for a workload, but does not say onboarding assembles inference-engine building blocks selected for a particular model.

r002.rationale: It mentions precision as a serving choice, but does not identify numerical errors from assembling inference-engine components as a possible cause of accuracy degradation.

r003.rationale: Load testing and monitoring are discussed, but the response does not state that capabilities layered on raw inference need correctness validation for each model.
